Click once per layer, top to bottom, as each part is spoken.

Context. Highest disaster risk among 193 countries. Taglish posts for help outnumber what responders can read.

Bottleneck. Earlier Philippine models did one task each. The Urdaneta City system does both but sends posts to OpenAI, which adds a third party under the Data Privacy Act.

Problem. One local model is cheaper, but it can suffer negative transfer. Optimizers try to fix this, yet studies disagree on whether they help.

Research Question. Read the full research question aloud.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the objectives and scope.

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

General objective. Compare 13 multi-task optimizers in negative transfer and training cost on Taglish disaster tweets, and examine how the two relate.

The first specific objective covers Objectives 1 and 2 in Chapter 1. Construct a dataset labeled for both tasks, measure inter-annotator agreement, and measure single-task baselines.

The second covers Objectives 3 and 4. Measure training time and peak memory of each optimizer, then test which of the 12 differ from equal weighting in negative transfer.

Scope. Tropical cyclones that crossed the Philippines from 2020 to 2026. Only humanitarian classification and named entity recognition. Thirteen multi-task optimizers, with equal weighting as the reference. All 15 models use one encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, trained on one laptop.

Exclusions, if asked. Other languages, other hazards, other platforms, images and video, other tasks, large language models, and deployment.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the literature and baselines.
:::

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

Ali et al. (2026). The closest work. A two-task model on English disaster tweets. Only two optimizers were compared, fixed task weights and uncertainty weighting, with no training time or memory.

Caoile and Aviles (2025). The Urdaneta City system from slide 2. Local text and both tasks, but it sends the text to OpenAI.

Kurin et al. (2022). Six optimizers compared, equal weighting, MGDA, IMTL, PCGrad, GradDrop, and random loss weighting. No clear advantage was found, but only on image and robot tasks. Training time was reported, but not memory.

Gap, stated aloud after the last row. No study combines Taglish text, both tasks, several optimizers, and measured training time and memory.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the methodology.
:::

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

Theoretical value. The results add a new language and domain to the debate on whether specialized optimizers outperform equal weighting. The two tasks differ in type, since one labels each word and the other labels the whole tweet. Gama and Grassi (2026) suggest that optimizers may matter more when tasks differ in this way.

Practical benefits. The measured training time and peak memory can guide developers who choose an optimizer for limited hardware. A single model that runs on a local government unit's own computers avoids sending posts to a third party. This is a possible use, not something the study tests.

Deliverables. The labeled dataset may be shared only in a form that complies with the Data Privacy Act and the terms of X. The labeling guidelines, code, and benchmark results are released.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the software artifact.

```{=html}
  </div>
```

```{=html}
    <svg viewBox="0 0 500 200" preserveAspectRatio="none">
      <rect width="500" height="200" fill="#f3f3f3"/>
      <path d="M300,0 C280,40 330,70 310,110 C290,150 340,170 320,200" fill="none" stroke="#c9d6e3" stroke-width="10"/>
      <path d="M0,60 L500,90 M0,150 L500,130 M120,0 L150,200 M420,0 L400,200" fill="none" stroke="#dddddd" stroke-width="4"/>
      <text x="40" y="40">Quezon City</text>
      <text x="40" y="185">Pasig</text>
      <text x="400" y="55">Marikina</text>
    </svg>

    <span class="pin c-caution" style="left:48%;top:22%"></span>
    <span class="pin c-request" style="left:30%;top:68%"></span>
    <span class="pin c-displaced" style="left:60%;top:78%"></span>
    <span class="pin c-request seed" style="left:76%;top:46%"></span>
    <div class="legend">
      <span><i class="c-request"></i>Requests</span>
      <span><i class="c-damage"></i>Damage</span>
      <span><i class="c-caution"></i>Caution</span>
      <span><i class="c-displaced"></i>Displaced</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="dash-feed" id="dash-feed">
    <div class="post shown cat-on ent-on">
      <div class="meta">@juan_mkna · now</div>
      <div class="text">Grabe na baha dito sa <mark class="e-loc">Brgy. Malanday, Marikina</mark>! Need po namin ng <mark class="e-res">rescue</mark>, may senior at baby dito. Pls help</div>
      <div class="tags">
        <span class="cat c-request">Requests or urgent needs</span>
        <span class="ent-key e-loc">LOCATION</span>
        <span class="ent-key e-res">RESCUE</span>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<script>
(() => {
  const tweets = [
    { user: "@juan_mkna", cat: "request", label: "Requests or urgent needs", x: 76, y: 46,
      text: "Grabe na baha dito sa [Brgy. Malanday, Marikina|loc]! Need po namin ng [rescue|res], may senior at baby dito. Pls help" },
    { user: "@kat_qc", cat: "damage", label: "Infrastructure and utility damage", x: 30, y: 26,
      text: "Bumagsak yung poste sa [Katipunan Ave|loc], wala pang kuryente. Sana ma-ayos na ng [Meralco|org]" },
    { user: "@pasig_updates", cat: "caution", label: "Caution and advice", x: 18, y: 80,
      text: "[PAGASA|org]: Signal No. 3 na sa [Pasig|loc]. Iwasan muna lumabas at mag-ingat sa baha" },
    { user: "@ate_rosa", cat: "displaced", label: "Displaced people and evacuations", x: 58, y: 62,
      text: "Nasa evacuation center na kami sa [Rosario Elem. School|loc], [200 families|dis] na dito" }
  ];
  const keys = { loc: "LOCATION", res: "RESCUE", org: "ORGANIZATION", dis: "DISPLACED" };
  const feed = document.getElementById("dash-feed");
  const map = document.getElementById("dash-map");
  const posts = document.getElementById("dash-posts");
  const urgent = document.getElementById("dash-urgent");
  let timers = [], index = 0, added = [];

  const later = (ms, fn) => timers.push(setTimeout(fn, ms));
  const stop = () => { timers.forEach(clearTimeout); timers = []; };

  function card(t) {
    const types = [];
    const html = t.text.replace(/\[([^|\]]+)\|(\w+)\]/g, (m, word, type) => {
      if (!types.includes(type)) types.push(type);
      return `<mark class="e-${type}">${word}</mark>`;
    });
    const el = document.createElement("div");
    el.className = "post";
    el.innerHTML = `<div class="meta">${t.user} · now</div><div class="text">${html}</div>` +
      `<div class="tags"><span class="cat c-${t.cat}">${t.label}</span>` +
      types.map(k => `<span class="ent-key e-${k}">${keys[k]}</span>`).join("") + `</div>`;
    return el;
  }

  function reset() {
    map.querySelectorAll(".seed").forEach(p => p.remove());
    added.forEach(p => p.remove());
    added = [];
    posts.textContent = 128;
    urgent.textContent = 23;
    feed.innerHTML = "";
    index = 0;
  }

  function step() {
    const t = tweets[index];
    const el = card(t);
    feed.querySelectorAll(".post").forEach(p => p.classList.add("old"));
    feed.prepend(el);
    while (feed.children.length > 2) feed.lastChild.remove();
    later(50, () => el.classList.add("shown"));
    later(1200, () => el.classList.add("cat-on"));
    later(2200, () => el.classList.add("ent-on"));
    later(3400, () => {
      const pin = document.createElement("span");
      pin.className = `pin c-${t.cat} drop`;
      pin.style.left = t.x + "%";
      pin.style.top = t.y + "%";
      map.insertBefore(pin, map.querySelector(".legend"));
      added.push(pin);
      posts.textContent = +posts.textContent + 1;
      if (t.cat === "request") urgent.textContent = +urgent.textContent + 1;
    });
    later(6000, () => {
      index += 1;
      if (index === tweets.length) reset();
      step();
    });
  }

  // Runs the loop only while this slide is on screen
  const section = map.closest("section");
  const printing = /print-pdf/.test(location.search);
  let active = false;
  setInterval(() => {
    const now = section.classList.contains("present") && !printing;
    if (now === active) return;
    active = now;
    stop();
    if (active) {
      reset();
      later(600, step);
    }
  }, 200);
})();
</script>
```
:::::
::::::

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

Architecture, top row. The benchmarking system. Data preparation collects tweets through the X API, cleans them, keeps the Taglish tweets, labels both tasks with two annotators, and splits the data. Training trains the 15 models with three seeds each and records training time and peak memory. Evaluation scores the saved models on the test set, computes F1-scores and negative transfer, and runs the two-way ANOVA and Tukey's HSD test.

Architecture, bottom row. The prototype web application. The interface runs in a web browser. The server runs the trained multi-task model with PyTorch. The database stores the posts, their labels, and their status. Everything runs on one computer, so posts are not sent to an outside service.

Tech stack. Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.8 with CUDA 12.8 on Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL 2. The laptop has an Intel Core i5-13500HX, 32 GB of memory, and an RTX 4060 with 8 GB. An internet connection is needed only to collect tweets and download the encoder and libraries.

Prototype demo. The animation plays by itself and loops through four posts, one for each of four categories. For each post, the model assigns its category, marks its entities, and the location becomes a pin on the map. The tweet, the map, and the counts are made up for this mockup. The prototype is not tested with DRRMO staff or during actual disasters.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the testing and evaluation plan.
:::

## Testing Method & Metrics {.vcenter}

::::: compare
| Metric | Measure | Tool |
|:-------|:--------|:-----|
| Accuracy | Macro-F1, span-level F1 | scikit-learn, seqeval |
| Negative transfer | F1 change from single-task | Single-task baselines |
| Speed | Training time per step | Python timer |
| Memory | Peak GPU memory (MiB) | PyTorch memory stats |
| Significance | Two-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD | SciPy |
| Prototype | Pass or fail per use case | Functional test cases |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,42,34]"}
:::::

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

Accuracy. Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, which gives each category equal weight. Named entity recognition is scored with span-level micro-F1, in which an entity counts as correct only when its boundaries and type both match.

Negative transfer. The change in F1 of each multi-task model from the single-task model of the same task, averaged over the two tasks.

Speed and memory. The time of every training step is recorded with a Python timer that waits for the graphics processor. Peak memory is read from PyTorch at the end of each run. nvidia-smi checks that the laptop did not slow down from heat.

Significance. A two-way ANOVA with the optimizer and the seed as factors, then Tukey's HSD to compare each optimizer with equal weighting.

Prototype. Each use case is tested with an input, an expected result, and the actual result. The prototype is not evaluated with DRRMO staff, because the research questions concern the optimizers.

Test data. All 15 models are scored on the same held-out test set, 14% of the labeled tweets, and each model is trained with three random seeds.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] presents the timeline.
:::

## Technical Risks & Backup Plans {.vcenter}

::: compare
| Risk | Backup Plan |
|:-----|:------------|
| Past cyclone tweets not accessible | Collect tweets from upcoming cyclones |
| Low annotator agreement | Revise guidelines before next batch |
| Optimizer code bugs | Test each optimizer on small examples |
| Optimizer exceeds 8 GB memory | Switch all models to parameter-efficient fine-tuning |
| Laptop slows from heat | Repeat the affected run |
| Prototype use case fails | Fix and retest before the defense |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}
:::

::: notes
Presenter [name], about 2 minutes.

Past cyclone tweets not accessible. Searching older tweets may require a higher X API tier. If past events cannot be accessed, tweets are collected from new tropical cyclones as they occur within the study period, and existing Philippine disaster tweet collections are checked for Taglish tweets that can be relabeled.

Low annotator agreement. When kappa falls below .61 or span F1 below .74, the guidelines are revised before the next batch, as Tabuzo et al. did.

Optimizer code bugs. Each optimizer is tested on small examples worked out by hand, for example that PCGrad leaves two gradients that do not conflict unchanged.

Optimizer exceeds 8 GB memory. Optimizers that store a gradient for each task need the most memory. The pilot run checks memory first. If an optimizer does not fit, all 15 models switch from full fine-tuning to parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which trains only a small part of the model instead of the whole encoder, for example with LoRA. The per-task gradients then become much smaller. The switch applies to every model so the comparison stays fair.

Laptop slows from heat. nvidia-smi records the temperature and clock speed every second, and a run that slowed down is repeated.

Prototype use case fails. The failing use case is fixed and its functional tests are run again.

Delays in general. The two-week buffer in late March absorbs repeated runs or late labeling.

Hand-off. [Next presenter] closes with the references and opens the floor for questions.
:::
